message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I own the EDIT area (`src/edit/`) and delegate to you the commands `corner`, `split` and `fillet`.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Edit ONLY `src/edit/corner.rs`, `src/edit/split.rs`, `src/edit/fillet.rs` (you may add files `src/edit/curves.rs` or `src/edit/ops_*.rs` for shared geometry, with their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`). Nothing else in the repo. Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/edit-ops/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell commands it can't verify (loops, heredocs, `cd` outside the worktree, `$(...)` feeding python): write Python scripts to files in /tmp and run them as `python3 /tmp/edit-ops/x.py`.

## Setup
You are in a git worktree. First make sure your HEAD contains commit 89ee1af ("Editing: module skeleton"): `git log --oneline -3`; if not, `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s).

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical float formatting (`1000.0`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies are printed sorted by main.rs: just return the Value), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order — key order matters, files are compared byte for byte after normalising GUIDs) + `library` (`{kind, name, guid}`); `alloc_id()` for new element ids; `find_guid`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID (a door's `host` is its wall's GUID, a dimension's `refs[].id`, a tag's `host`, a line's `view` and `style`).
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label when the project changed (`corner` that changes nothing makes no step, I saw).
- `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers with the original's texts: `` `at` [x, y] is required``, ``must be a point [x, y] in mm, got …``), `src/edit/common.rs` (`ids_param` — `ids`, else `id`, with the original's errors —, `resolve`, `r3` rounding to 0.001 mm, which the original does on computed coordinates — check where), `src/styles/phasing.rs` (`stamp_copy(pr, s.now_phase, s.now_option, &mut e)`: what a new element made from another gets of the session's phase/option — find out whether a split's new part gets it).
- Other areas are being written in parallel and are empty stubs now: ARCH (walls, doors, rooms…, and model rules such as "a door must fit its wall"), VIEWS (detail lines and their own commands offset/trim_extend/join_polyline/explode/vertex/convert_spline, dimensions, tags), READERS. Don't implement their commands or their model rules; if a refusal of the original comes from such a model rule (after the change), list it in your report. Your commands must work on project files made by the ORIGINAL.

## How to test
Build input projects with the original: `/workspace/executable run --script s.txt --save in.bimcraft` (e.g. `wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000]]}`, `wall {... "arc": 90}`, `door {"at": [2000,0]}`, `detail_line {"start": [0,0], "end": [4000,0]}`, `detail_line {"points": [[0,0],[1000,0],[1000,1000]], "arcs": [0, 90]}`, circles, ellipses, splines by `control` and by `fit` — see `/workspace/executable commands`). A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (`python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file [ids|categories]` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict) and `/tmp/edit-agent/probe.py in.bimcraft 'split {...}'` prints the reply and the element diff; use them, but don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. To compare with yours: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd 'split {…}' --save out.bimcraft` prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels must match exactly.

## Your commands
- `corner` (TR): "{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep". Seen: `corner {"ids": [100002, 100003]}` on two walls already meeting at (8000,0) replies `{"corner": [8000.0, 0.0]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `corner: `ids` takes two walls`.
- `split` (SL): "{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`". Seen: on a wall → `{"ids": [100002, 100036]}`; `split {"id": 5}` → `split: 5 is not a wall`; `{}` → `split: `id`, a wall or a detail line, is required`. Arcs walls split into two arcs.
- `fillet` (FL): "{ids: [a, b], radius} rounds the corner where two straight detail lines, or two straight walls, meet (or would, extended) with an arc of `radius` mm, in the first's line style or of the first's type: each is cut back to the arc (a wall's doors and windows stay where they stand in plan, as in `corner`, and only their offset along the wall changes)". Seen: two walls → `{"id": 100036, "ids": [100002, 100003]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `fillet: `ids` is two detail lines`.
For each: every error and the order of checks (wrong categories, same id twice, parallel lines, lines of different views, walls on different levels, `at` off the element, radius too big…), what happens to the doors and windows of a wall (offsets recomputed so they stand where they stood in plan; a door on the part split off moves to the new wall, its `host` changing), to other walls joined at the trimmed/extended ends (walls whose end is within 1 mm of another wall's end or line count as joined — find out whether corner/split/fillet stretch them), to dimensions and tags referring to a split wall or line, to the new element's fields (a copy of the original's fields, key order, GUID, `stamp_copy`?), the rounding of the results (r3?), arcs (walls with `arc`, detail lines with `through`/`arc`/`arcs`/`centre`…), and undo labels (`Trim/Extend to Corner`, `Split`, `Fillet Arc`; whether an unchanged result makes a step). Prioritise walls and straight detail lines; then arcs; then polylines, circles, ellipses and splines.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: your branch name and commit; per command what matches (tested with cmp.py) and what doesn't; what other areas must provide (model rules behind refusals…).

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

systemPrompt:
You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

content.content: 61: 3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. 77: 81: Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. 169: 207: them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and 229:| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do | 233:| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted | 246:| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo | 247:| Snaps and the ruler | Points picked while drawing stick to what the plan has there, as Revit's snaps do: the ends, middles and centres of walls (an arc's too), grids and components, the centres of columns, structural columns and footings with the corners and edge middles of their outlines (a round one's four quadrants), so a wall can start flush with a column's edge, and the corners of floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; where two straight walls or grids cross; the foot of the perpendicular from the last point to a straight wall or grid; and a wall's centre line, so a wall drawn onto it meets it. It also sticks to the anchors of notes, dimensions, tags, spot elevations, section and elevation marks, detail groups and repeating details; a camera's mark gives its eye and target, never the body, lens or name it is drawn with. Each shows its own marker and its name. A direction from the last point sticks to multiples of an angle (5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°; 15° by default), from east and from the line before it, so corners come out exact, sharp ones too: a dashed guide shows it, and where it crosses a wall or grid the point lands there. The line being drawn carries a ruler: graduations at round lengths, its length and its angle (at the corner it turns once there's a line before it, drawn as an arc). Manage > Snaps switches each snap and sets the angle steps, and Revit's SE, SM, SI, SC, SP and SN take one snap alone for the next point (SO none, SS back); Measure (ME) lays a ruler between two snapped points and reads its length, parts and angle; the `measure` command does the same. Each plan, section and elevation has a background grid, a main grid and a subgrid with their own spacing, divisions, colours and pens, turned by an angle, kept in the view's graphics and controlled by its template; Grid snapping (Manage > Snaps, or the grid menu in the view control bar) lands a free point on its crossings | 248:| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section | 265:| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) | 369:| Shafts | Architecture > Opening > Shaft: click two opposite corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected). It cuts the floors, ceilings and roofs on its way | 370:| Masses | Massing > Conceptual Mass > Mass (MS): click the footprint's corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected); Enter, or the first corner again, finishes. Before you do, the outline it would make shows, with its area. With a mass selected, Model by Face makes Mass Floors (MF: a floor at each level it crosses), Wall by Face (WB: a wall on each edge), Floor by Face (FB) and Roof by Face (RB) on its top face, and Update to Face (UF) makes what they made follow the mass again; Show Mass (MH) hides and shows masses in the view on screen. Properties shows its constraints, its Top Outline (corners as `x, y; x, y`, blank for none: typed, the mass is lofted), area, volume and gross floor area. View > Schedules lists Mass and Mass Floor schedules | 376:| Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. It turns and moves walls, columns, components, slabs, roofs, structural/MEP runs and detail geometry onto the reference in one undo step; hosted doors and windows slide along their wall. While sketching, align sketch lines to model edges or other sketch lines; joined endpoints follow, with sketch undo until Finish. Trim/Extend to Corner (TR): pick two walls on the parts to keep. Split Element (SL): click a wall where to cut it. Offset (OF): point to a wall, and a copy goes to the cursor's side at the Options Bar's distance | 377:| Dimension, tag | Annotate > Aligned (DI): pick parallel references, each the line nearest the cursor (a wall's face, centre line or end, a door's or window's centre or jamb, a grid), or endpoints (a wall's end or corner, a line's or a grid's end), which a square marks, then click away from them where the dimension line goes; more picks make a chain. Linear: pick endpoints, then click where it goes, horizontal or vertical as the cursor lies; the Options Bar's Place (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them) lays either tool's dimension. Angular: pick two lines that meet, then click where the arc goes; the angle on that side. Radial and Diameter: pick a round column, a curved wall, a circle or an arc, then click where it goes. Arc Length: pick a curved wall or an arc, then, to measure part of it, two ends on it, then click where the dimension's arc goes. Edit Type on a dimension opens Dimension Type Properties; a double click on one of its numbers opens Dimension Text, that segment's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, or text in its place. Selected, a dimension shows a padlock under each segment and EQ past its end: a click locks a segment at its length, or keeps the segments equal, and what it measures to then moves with what moves, as in Revit. Annotate > Tag by Category (TG): click any element with a place in a plan (a door or window, a wall, a column, a component, a floor, ceiling or roof, a room, a beam or pipe, a stair) to tag it with its type, a door's or window's with its mark, a room's with its name, or with any other field its schedule has (Height, Area, a project parameter) typed in Label in the Options Bar, with a leader when it says so; Tag All tags the doors and windows of the view not tagged yet. Drag a dimension or a tag to move it | 378:| Spot elevations, text | Annotate > Spot Elevation (EL): click a floor, a roof, a stair or a wall in plan, and it reads the height of its top there, following it; in a section, click a point to mark its height. Annotate > Text (TX): type the note in the Options Bar (`\n` breaks a line), then click its top left corner, in a plan, a section or on a sheet; Properties sets its size and angle | 390:| Snaps and the ruler | While a tool picks points, what a click would land on is marked: a square for an end, a triangle for a middle, a cross for a crossing, a circle for a centre, a right angle for a perpendicular, a diamond for the nearest point of a wall, a dot on an angle guide, each named beside it. Past the last point a dashed guide runs at the angle the direction sticks to (from east, and from the line before), and the new line wears a ruler: its length and angle read beside it, and at a corner the angle between the two walls, shown as an arc, so a 60° corner is easy to hit. Offset has `length`, `count` (2–9), `distance`; waves/zigzags have `length`, `frequency` (cycles per segment), `amplitude`; text has `length`, `size`, `text`, in bundled IBM Plex Sans, flowing along curves.     t = math.radians(th_deg)

    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)

S = (2000.0, -3000.0)
E = (2000.0, 3000.0)
th = 73.739795292
target = 36.86989764599999


def centre_a(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    d = c / 2 / math.tan(t / 2)
    return (mx + nx * d, my + ny * d), r


def centre_b(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / (2 * math.sin(t / 2))
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    h = math.sqrt(max(r * r - c * c / 4, 0))
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    return (mx + nx * h, my + ny * h), r


def centre_c(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    nx, ny = -dy, dx
    k = 0.5 / math.tan(t / 2)
    return (mx + nx * k, my + ny * k), r


for name, cf in (('a', centre_a), ('b', centre_b), ('c', centre_c)):
    C, r = cf(S, E, th)
    for P in ((3000.0, 0.0),):
        sx, sy = P[0] - C[0], P[1] - C[1]
        ex, ey = E[0] - C[0], E[1] - C[1]
        a_s = math.atan2(sy, sx)
        a_e = math.atan2(ey, ex)
        a0 = math.atan2(S[1] - C[1], S[0] - C[0])
        cands = {
            'ae-as': math.degrees(a_e - a_s),
            'deg diff': math.degrees(a_e) - math.degrees(a_s),
            'atan2(cross,dot)': math.degrees(math.atan2(sx * ey - sy * ex, sx * ex + sy * ey)),
            'acos': math.degrees(math.acos((sx * ex + sy * ey) / (math.hypot(sx, sy) * math.hypot(ex, ey)))),
            'th-(as-a0)': th - math.degrees(a_s - a0),

            '2atan': None,
        }
        # bulge: sagitta via midpoint of arc

        mid = ((P[0] + E[0]) / 2, (P[1] + E[1]) / 2)
        dm = math.hypot(mid[0] - C[0], mid[1] - C[1])
        sag = r - dm

wall | Wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door | Door | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window | Window | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

dimension | Aligned Dimension | {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 1

tag | Tag by Category | {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

flip | Flip | {ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

modify | Modify | {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

move | Move | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves

detail_line | Detail Line | {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 

phase | Phasing | {name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. graphic_display_options | Graphic Display Options | {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has

phase | Phasing | {name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the firs

phase_filter | Phase Filter | {name, new?, existing?, demolished?, temporary?, delete?} a phase filter: how a view shows each status of what's in its phase, each `by-category` (as its category and the view's overrides say), `overridden` (as the project's overrides for that status say) or `not-displayed`. A project has Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New; any may change. A new one starts by category throughout. One in use by a view or a template can't be deleted. Replies with the filter

option | Design Options | {set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one o

import sys, json, math, random
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-ops')
from exp import build, run

random.seed(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 5)
samples = []
for i in range(int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 12):
    # A from s to e; corner beyond the start: B crosses A's line before its start
    s = [round(random.uniform(-5000, 5000), 3), round(random.uniform(-5000, 5000), 3)]
    ang = random.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)
    L = random.uniform(3000, 9000)
    e = [round(s[0] + L * math.cos(ang), 3), round(s[1] + L * math.sin(ang), 3)]
    ext = random.uniform(200, 3000)
    c = [s[0] - ext * math.cos(ang), s[1] - ext * math.sin(ang)]
    bang = ang + random.uniform(0.3, 2.8)
    b0 = [round(c[0] + 1000 * math.cos(bang), 3), round(c[1] + 1000 * math.sin(bang), 3)]
    b1 = [round(c[0] + 4000 * math.cos(bang), 3), round(c[1] + 4000 * math.sin(bang), 3)]
    cmds = ['wall {"points": [%s, %s]}' % (json.dumps(s), json.dumps(e)), 'wall {"points": [%s, %s]}' % (json.dumps(b0), json.dumps(b1))]
    for k in range(3):
        u = random.uniform(0.2, 0.8)
        p = [round(s[0] + (e[0] - s[0]) * u, 3), round(s[1] + (e[1] - s[1]) * u, 3)]
        cmds.append('door {"at": %s}' % json.dumps(p))
    try:
        text = build(cmds)
    except Exception as ex:
        continue
    ok, rep, proj = run(text, ['corner {"ids": [100002, 100003]}'])
    if not ok:
        print('ERR', rep)
        continue
    A = json.loads(text)['elements']
    B = proj['elements']

import json, math, sys
from fractions import Fraction as F
rows = [list(map(float, l.split())) for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip()]


def unit(s, e):
    d = [e[0] - s[0], e[1] - s[1]]
    l = math.hypot(d[0], d[1])
    return [d[0] * (1 / l), d[1] * (1 / l)]


def station(s, e, p):
    u = unit(s, e)
    q = [p[0] - s[0], p[1] - s[1]]
    return q[0] * u[0] + q[1] * u[1]


def along(s, e, off):
    u = unit(s, e)
    return [s[0] + u[0] * off, s[1] + u[1] * off]


def exact(s0, e0, s1, e1, off):
    # exact rational except sqrt: use high precision via Fraction of float sqrt (approx)
    d0 = [F(e0[0]) - F(s0[0]), F(e0[1]) - F(s0[1])]
    d1 = [F(e1[0]) - F(s1[0]), F(e1[1]) - F(s1[1])]
    import decimal
    decimal.getcontext().prec = 60
    L0 = decimal.Decimal(d0[0] * d0[0] + d0[1] * d0[1]).sqrt() if False else None
    return None


for v in rows:
    s0, e0, s1, e1, off, target = v[0:2], v[2:4], v[4:6], v[6:8], v[8], v[9]
    got = station(s1, e1, along(s0, e0, off))
    if got != target:
        # true value with decimals
        import decimal
        D = decimal.Decimal
        decimal.getcontext().prec = 50
        d0 = [D(e0[0]) - D(s0[0]), D(e0[1]) - D(s0[1])]
        L0 = (d0[0] * d0[0] + d0[1] * d0[1]).sqrt()
        P = [D(s0[0]) + d0[0] / L0 * D(off), D(s0[1]) + d0[1] / L0 * D(off)]
        d1 = [D(e1[0]) - D(s1[0]), D(e1[1]) - D(s1[1])]
        L1 = (d1[0] * d1[0] + d1[1] * d1[1]).sqrt()
        tv = ((P[0] - D(s1[0])) * d1[0] + (P[1] - D(s1[1])) * d1[1]) / L1
        ulp = math.ulp(target)
        print('got %r target %r true %s  got-true %.2f ulp  target-true %.2f ulp' % (got, target, str(tv)[:22], float(D(got) - tv) / ulp, float(D(target) - tv) / ulp))

import json, math
rows = json.load(open('/tmp/edit-ops/an18.json'))


def arc_geo(s, e, deg):
    t = math.radians(deg); ch = (e[0] - s[0], e[1] - s[1]); l = math.hypot(*ch)
    r = l / 2 / abs(math.sin(t / 2)); m = ((s[0] + e[0]) / 2, (s[1] + e[1]) / 2); n = (-ch[1] / l, ch[0] / l); d = l / 2 / math.tan(t / 2)
    c = (m[0] + n[0] * d, m[1] + n[1] * d)
    a0 = math.atan2(s[1] - c[1], s[0] - c[0])
    return c, r, a0, t


def dist(a, b):
    return math.hypot(a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1])


stats = {}
for row in rows:
    b = row['before']
    a = row['after']
    li = 0 if 'arc' not in b[0] else 1
    ai = 1 - li
    L, A = b[li], b[ai]
    c, r, a0, th = arc_geo(A['start'], A['end'], A['arc'])
    p0, p1 = L['start'], L['end']
    d = (p1[0] - p0[0], p1[1] - p0[1]); ll = math.hypot(*d); u = (d[0] / ll, d[1] / ll)
    tf = (c[0] - p0[0]) * u[0] + (c[1] - p0[1]) * u[1]
    f = (p0[0] + u[0] * tf, p0[1] + u[1] * tf)
    h2 = r * r - dist(f, c) ** 2
    if h2 <= 0:
        continue
    h = math.sqrt(h2)
    X = [(f[0] - u[0] * h, f[1] - u[1] * h), (f[0] + u[0] * h, f[1] + u[1] * h)]
    # which was chosen: the point the moved ends sit at
    moved = []
    for k in ('start', 'end'):
        if a[li][k] != L[k]:
            moved.append(a[li][k])
        if a[ai][k] != A[k]:
            moved.append(a[ai][k])
    if not moved:
        continue
    q = moved[0]
    ch = 0 if dist(q, X[0]) < dist(q, X[1]) else 1
    keep = row['keep']
    if keep is None:
        kl = ((p0[0] + p1[0]) / 2, (p0[1] + p1[1]) / 2)
        mid = a0 + th / 2
        ka = (c[0] + r * math.cos(mid), c[1] + r * math.sin(mid))
    else:
        kl = keep[li]
        ka = keep[ai]

    def apar(p):
        ang = math.atan2(p[1] - c[1], p[0] - c[0])
        return ((ang - a0) * (1 if th > 0 else -1)) % (2 * math.pi)

    rules = {
        'near line keep': 0 if dist(kl, X[0]) < dist(kl, X[1]) else 1,
        'near arc keep': 0 if dist(ka, X[0]) < dist(ka, X[1]) else 1,
        'min sum': 0 if dist(kl, X[0]) + dist(ka, X[0]) < dist(kl, X[1]) + dist(ka, X[1]) else 1,
        'near first keep': 0 if dist(keep[0] if keep else (kl if li == 0 else ka), X[0]) < dist(keep[0] if keep else (kl if li == 0 else ka), X[1]) else 1,
    }
    for k, v in rules.items():
        stats.setdefault(k, [0, 0])
        stats[k][0] += (v == ch)
        stats[k][1] += 1
for k, v in stats.items():
    print(k, v)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fz3.py file n seed: corner/split/fillet on every pair of walls (and lines) of a project file."""
import sys, json, random
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-ops')
from exp import ORIG, MINE
import t as T

src = sys.argv[1]
n = int(sys.argv[2])
random.seed(int(sys.argv[3]))
d = json.load(open(src))
walls = [int(k) for k, v in d['elements'].items() if v['category'] == 'wall']
lines = [int(k) for k, v in d['elements'].items() if v['category'] == 'line']
tests = []
for _ in range(n):
    kind = random.choice(['corner', 'corner', 'fillet', 'split'])
    pool = walls if (random.random() < 0.7 or not lines) else lines
    if len(pool) < 2:
        continue
    a, b = random.sample(pool, 2)
    if kind == 'corner':
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            tests.append('corner {"ids": [%d, %d]}' % (a, b))
        else:
            k = [[random.randint(-3000, 11000), random.randint(-3000, 9000)] for _ in range(2)]
            tests.append('corner {"ids": [%d, %d], "keep": %s}' % (a, b, json.dumps(k)))
    elif kind == 'fillet':
        tests.append('fillet {"ids": [%d, %d], "radius": %s}' % (a, b, random.choice([100, 500, 1000, 2500, 123.456])))
    else:
        e = d['elements'][str(a)]
        if 'start' not in e:
            continue
        s, t = e['start'], e['end']
        u = random.uniform(0, 1)
        p = [round(s[0] + (t[0] - s[0]) * u + random.uniform(-50, 50), 3), round(s[1] + (t[1] - s[1]) * u + random.uniform(-50, 50), 3)]
        tests.append('split {"id": %d, "at": %s}' % (a, p))
total = same = 0
rules = ("doesn't fit wall", 'too short (', 'is not a usable number', 'mm long or less', ' overlap in wall')
ruled = 0
for c in tests:
    code, out, err, proj = T.run(ORIG, src, [c])
    mc, mo, me, mp = T.run(MINE, src, [c])
    ok = (code == mc and T.norm(out) == T.norm(mo) and T.norm(err) == T.norm(me) and T.norm(proj or '') == T.norm(mp or ''))
    total += 1
    if not ok and code != 0 and mc == 0 and any(r in err for r in rules):
        ruled += 1
        same += 1
        continue
    if ok:
        same += 1
        continue
    print('DIFF', c)
    print('    orig:', (out.splitlines()[1] if code == 0 else err.strip())[:300])
    print('    mine:', (mo.splitlines()[1] if mc == 0 else me.strip())[:300])
    if proj and mp:
        for l in T.diff(json.loads(proj), json.loads(mp))[:8]:
            print('      m~', l[:300])
print('%d/%d same (%d refused by other areas\' rules)' % (same, total, ruled))

            L = (d[0] ** 2 + d[1] ** 2) ** 0.5
            n = (-d[1] / L, d[0] / L)
            p = (round(A[0] + d[0] * u + n[0] * dl, 4), round(A[1] + d[1] * u + n[1] * dl, 4))
            pts.append((u, dl, p))
            cmds.append('split {"id": 100002, "at": [%r, %r]}' % p)

content.text:
I implemented `corner`, `split` and `fillet` on branch `worktree-agent-ae2e58ef39e2084a3` (HEAD `f6c591b`, three commits on top of `89ee1af`). Walls and straight detail lines match the original in everything I tested. Arcs, curves and some line splits still differ in the last digits of unrounded numbers. Two other areas also have to supply model rules before every case matches.

The code is in `src/edit/corner.rs`, `split.rs` and `fillet.rs`, plus four helper files I added (`ops_geom.rs`, `ops_lines.rs`, `ops_arcs.rs`, `ops_curves.rs`, with their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`). Results below are from the edit-agent probe scripts, `cmp.py`-style comparisons and my own random tests against the original. "Refused" below means the original stops with a model-rule error from another area, which this repo doesn't have yet.

**corner**
- **Walls:** all random tests match (280 cases, 76 refused by the other areas' rules), including every error text and the order of checks.
  - Without `keep`, each wall keeps the side its midpoint is on; a keep point exactly at the corner keeps the start side.
  - The moved end becomes `old + (corner − old)`, so stored coordinates carry the same float noise as the original's.
  - Joined walls follow, and only for a wall that actually changed (first wall, then second):
    - An end within 1 mm of the old end snaps to the new end, even when that end didn't move.
    - An end within 1 mm of the old segment goes to where its own line crosses the new line (rounded to 0.001 mm).
    - Same level only, no chain reaction.
  - Doors and windows keep their plan position.
  - Walls on different levels are not refused, and a corner that changes nothing makes no undo step.
- **Lines:** straight lines all match (225 cases). With an arc, the structure matches: which crossing is used (the one nearest the midpoint of the two keep points), which end moves, the rounded points. The new `arc` value differs in the last digits in about half the cases.
- **Known gaps:**
  - About 3% of door offsets after a corner that moves an oblique wall's start differ by 1–2 ULP.
  - For nearly parallel lines, where the original starts saying "don't meet" isn't pinned down; I refuse only when the corner is more than 1e9 mm out.

**split**
- **Straight walls:** all match (451 cases).
  - `at` must be within thickness/2 + 100 mm of the wall's centre line, which accounts for location lines.
  - The cut position is rounded to 0.001 mm and must be more than 1 mm from each end.
  - A door or window is "in the way" if |offset − t| < width/2 − 1.
  - The new part is a plain copy (no phase/option stamping). "Mass Face" is removed from both parts.
  - Openings past the cut move to the new wall: new host, offset − t.
  - Dimensions and tags are left alone.
- **Curved walls:** 297/312 match; the misses are float-level door offsets on the second part.
- **Detail lines:** errors and structure match for straight lines and for every other shape I tested.
  - Polylines become a line or a shorter polyline; `arcs` is dropped when all zero.
  - Closed polylines, circles and whole ellipses reply `"opened": true`.
  - Partial ellipses split their span; splines split by knot insertion.
- **Why curve splits miss:** the original finds the nearest point with an iterative search I couldn't reproduce. Its unrounded results only match mine at exact points; about half of oblique straight-line splits also differ in the last digits.
- **Fitted splines and error distances:**
  - Fitted splines are only approximated.
  - The "it passes … mm" distance for curves can differ in the second decimal.

**fillet**
- **Walls:** all match (240 cases).
  - The arc wall copies the first wall, gets `arc` (9 decimals) in its field position, and is stamped with the session's phase/option where it holds none of its own.
  - Every opening's offset is recomputed and rounded to 0.001 mm.
  - A door left outside its part gives the "in the part … the fillet cuts away" error.
  - Each wall must keep more than 1 mm beyond the arc. No joined walls follow.
- **Lines:** 144/160 match; the misses are 1-ULP differences in `arc`.

**What other areas must provide**
- **ARCH** model rules seen behind refusals: "wall N: too short (X mm)", "door N: W mm wide at offset O doesn't fit wall M, L mm long", "door A and door B overlap in wall …", and "wall N x: V is not a usable number".
- **VIEWS** model rules: "line N: it is 1 mm long or less" and "dimension N: wall A isn't parallel to wall B; a dimension measures between parallel walls and grids". The second one fires when a corner stretches a joined wall.
- **For you:**
  - A `corner` on two detail lines makes an undo step even when nothing changes. I can't change `always_step`, so I added `corner::step_anyway()`; please add `"corner" => corner::step_anyway()` to `edit::always_step` in `mod.rs`.
  - The original replaces any library-entry GUID anywhere in a command's parameters with that entry's name, which is why messages show e.g. `got "Thin Lines"`. This is global in the original; I only do it for my three commands (`ops_geom::lib_names`).
  - `ops_geom::follow_joins` is the same joined-wall logic that `move {end}` uses in the original (I checked `move` with `end` on door offsets), so it could be reused for `move`.
